title: Dependency Injection Fundamentals
description: Learn what dependency injection is, why it matters, how to register services, and how to inject them into controllers and views.

terms.definition: A design pattern where objects receive their dependencies from an external container rather than creating them internally.
Any class registered in the DI container that can be injected into another class.
The built-in ASP.NET Core mechanism that manages service creation and lifetime.
Code where a class directly creates instances of its dependencies using new — hard to test or change.
Code where dependencies are injected via interfaces — easy to test and swap implementations.

data.text: Before DI, a controller might directly create its own repository. This is **tightly coupled**: if you ever want to swap the repository implementation, you must edit every class that uses it.

data.title: Tightly coupled — controller creates its own dependency
data.content: A controller that directly instantiates a Repository — hard to test and hard to change

data.title: Why is this a problem?
data.text: If ProductRepository changes its constructor signature or you replace it with a database-backed version, you must edit every controller (and test) that uses it directly.
DI reverses control: instead of the controller creating its dependency, ASP.NET Core's **IoC container** creates and injects it. The controller only declares what it needs — via its constructor.

data.title: Two steps to apply DI
items: Depend on an interface (or a concrete type) — never use new inside the class.
Register the mapping in Program.cs so the container knows which implementation to provide.

data.title: Loosely coupled controller — DI via constructor
data.content: The controller now depends on an interface; the container injects the real implementation

data.text: The registration in Program.cs tells the container: "Whenever someone asks for `IProductRepository`, give them `ProductRepository`."

data.title: Registering the service in Program.cs
data.content: Mapping an interface to its implementation in the DI container

data.text: If your class doesn't implement an interface, you can still register it directly. The container resolves dependencies by the concrete type.

data.title: Registering a concrete class with no interface
data.content: Registering a single-type service — the container creates an instance of ProductSum directly

data.text: For advanced scenarios, register a factory lambda. This lets you write custom logic — for example, choosing a different repository based on the current environment.

data.title: Factory registration — different implementation per environment
data.content: Using a lambda to decide which repository implementation to create at runtime

data.text: A dependency chain occurs when one service depends on another, which in turn depends on another. ASP.NET Core resolves the entire chain automatically — you just register each link.

data.caption: How ASP.NET Core resolves a dependency chain: Controller → Repository → Storage
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[HomeController] -->|depends on| B[IRepository]
    B -->|implemented by| C[Repository]
    C -->|depends on| D[IStorage]
    D -->|implemented by| E[Storage]
    style A fill:#4CAF50,color:#fff
    style C fill:#2196F3,color:#fff

data.title: Resolving a dependency chain in Program.cs
data.content: Registering each link in the chain so the container can build the full object graph

data.text: Razor Views can receive services directly using the `@inject` directive. This is useful when a view needs data that isn't provided by the controller.

data.title: Injecting IConfiguration into a Razor view
data.content: Using @inject to access appsettings values directly in a Razor view

data.text: Sometimes only one action method needs a service, not the whole controller. Use the `[FromServices]` attribute on the action parameter to resolve it directly from the container — avoiding unnecessary constructor injection.

data.title: [FromServices] on a single action method
data.content: Resolving a service only for the action method that needs it

data.title: Exercise: Decouple a Controller
data.description: You are given a controller that directly instantiates a ProductRepository with new. Refactor it to use constructor injection via an interface.
steps: Define an IProductRepository interface with a GetAll() method.
Replace the new ProductRepository() call in the controller with a constructor parameter of type IProductRepository.
Register the mapping in Program.cs using AddTransient.
Confirm the controller no longer references ProductRepository directly in its constructor.
data.expectedOutcome: A controller that depends only on IProductRepository, with the real implementation provided by the DI container at runtime.

items.text: I can explain why tightly coupled code is hard to maintain and test
items.hint: Think about what happens when you swap one dependency for another

items.text: I know the two steps to apply DI in a controller
I can register a service using AddTransient, AddScoped, and AddSingleton
I understand when to use a factory registration
items.hint: When you need custom logic to choose an implementation at runtime

items.text: I can use @inject in a Razor view and [FromServices] on an action method

items.question: Do I always need an interface for DI?
items.answer: No. You can inject concrete types directly using the single-type registration overload (AddTransient<ProductService>). Interfaces are a best practice for testability, not a hard requirement.

items.question: Where else can I inject services besides controllers?
items.answer: Services can be injected into Razor views (@inject), into action methods ([FromServices]), into custom middleware (constructor injection), and into other services (constructor injection).

items.question: What if I forget to register a service?
items.answer: ASP.NET Core throws an InvalidOperationException at runtime when it cannot resolve the dependency. The error message names the service type that is missing from the container.

items.question: Is DI only for controllers?
items.answer: No. DI works anywhere the container can provide an instance — controllers, views, middleware, even other registered services. Any class that the container creates can receive constructor-injected dependencies.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: DI lets ASP.NET Core automatically supply object dependencies so classes don't create them with new.
Tight coupling means hard-to-test code; DI enforces loose coupling through interfaces.
Register services in Program.cs with AddTransient, AddScoped, or AddSingleton.
Use a factory lambda when you need runtime logic to choose an implementation.
Use @inject in Razor views and [FromServices] on individual action methods when only part of a class needs a service.
data.takeaway: DI is the backbone of testable, maintainable ASP.NET Core applications. Register services once, and the container handles the rest.
